tagline.text: A forested city park and a tree house loved by Zamboanga locals

location.label: Location
location.text: Pasonanca Road, Barangay Pasonanca, Zamboanga City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–600 (per person, covering transport, admissions and snacks)

children.text: Pasonanca Park is a forested city park about
7km

north of downtown Zamboanga, home to a tree house built in 1960, a butterfly garden, swimming pools and a campground. The park itself is free to enter and only the attractions inside charge small fees, so it makes an easy half-day stop during a city tour.
Pasonanca Park is a public park in Barangay Pasonanca, Zamboanga City. It sits on higher ground about
7km

north of the city center, so it has more trees and cooler air than the seafront downtown. Locals come here for weekend family picnics and for Boy Scout and student events, so it feels more like a neighborhood retreat than a tourist attraction.

The park's roots go back to the early 20th century. According to Wikipedia, construction began in 1912 under General John J. Pershing, then Governor of the Moro Province, and Thomas Hanley, who came from the United States, did the original layout. The park was reportedly completed under Governor Frank Carpenter. One travel blog says it opened to the public in the 1910s.

There are several things to see scattered around the grounds. The most famous is the tree house, and La Jardin de Maria Clara Lobregat has orchids, roses, a butterfly garden and an aviary with parrots, turkeys and eagles. Inside the garden complex is a small museum, El Museo de Zamboanga, and the grounds also hold three swimming pools, the Camp Limbaga campground, an amphitheater and a convention center. Higher up, Mt. Pulong Bato has a Way of the Cross and a viewpoint.

It is not the same as the similarly named Pasonanca Natural Park. The natural park is a protected area of about 12,107 hectares managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, and it was inaugurated as the 52nd ASEAN Heritage Park in May 2024. The park in this guide is the city park in the village that gave the natural park its name, and it is the one an ordinary traveler can stroll through in half a day. First-time visitors should know that this is an old public park, not a polished theme park. Upkeep varies from facility to facility and signage may be sparse. In return, entry is free, facility fees are only a few pesos, and you get a close look at how Zamboanga residents relax. It works well for a slow walk with kids, or as a shady rest before or after seeing the seafront downtown.

This is the most photographed building in the park. It was built in April 1960 as the Youth Citizenship Training Center and today is run like a rentable lodge. One guide advises contacting the city government's administration office first about overnight stays or rentals; we could not confirm the rate, so please check locally.

blocks.title: La Jardin de Maria Clara Lobregat

children.text: A garden park named after a late mayor. It has orchids and roses, and the aviary holds parrots, turkeys and eagles. Facilities inside reportedly charge small admission fees, usually around

Part of the garden complex, it is described as a small mini-zoo grouped with the aviary and charging a small fee. It makes a short, pleasant stop with children. The number of butterflies can vary with the season and upkeep.
The park has three public pools: an Olympic-size pool, a natural flowing pool, and a children's pool with four water slides. One travel blog lists pool admission at
for adults and

for children, and a 2023 guide also lists ₱10 with hours of Friday to Tuesday, 8:00-16:00 (closed Wednesday and Thursday). Admission was free for all of December 2025 by order of the mayor, so check the current fee and hours locally. Some visitor reviews, however, mention empty pools or cloudy water, so keep your expectations modest.
A small museum inside the Maria Clara Lobregat garden complex. It is reported to open Monday to Friday,
to
, and to close on weekends and holidays. Admission is described as
for adults and
for minors, students and seniors.

Used for Boy Scout events and camping, the grounds have a convention center and an amphitheater, with separate campsites for men and women. One account says the grounds commemorate 24 Filipino Boy Scouts who died in a 1963 accident in India. Group use may require advance booking. The area is also known as a scout ground with tepee-style structures from the 1960s, a tree house and a Rizal statue, and it hosts scout camps and jamborees.

Many local families spread out a packed lunch on the lawns and in the shelters. On the way to the park there are small eateries, sari-sari stores and charcoal-grilled barbecue stalls, so snacks are easy to find. Treat food as a light bite, and if hygiene worries you, choose freshly cooked dishes.
Above the park, a road lined with the 14 Stations of the Cross climbs Mt. Pulong Bato (about

high) to the Abong-Abong viewpoint. From the large cross at the top you can look down over the city. Visitors report taking a motorcycle taxi called habal-habal from the park entrance, so agree on the price before you ride. The area also has a memorial park called Freedom Park, and the burial site of the slain mayor Cesar Climaco is reported to be there. Confirm its location locally before you go.
Take a jeepney heading to Pasonanca from a downtown stop up to the park entrance. The ride usually takes
20–30 minutes
Start with the tree house while the morning air is cool, and take your photos.
Head to the Maria Clara Lobregat garden and walk through the orchid garden, the butterfly garden and the aviary.
On a weekday, drop in at El Museo de Zamboanga to see its local history displays.
Have lunch at a street stall or small eatery near the park.
Check the pools and, if you have children, let them splash for a while. If the pools look poor, rest on the lawn before heading down.
The park is small enough for a half day. If you are staying downtown, going up in the morning and coming back down after lunch is a sensible rhythm.

items.title: Full-day route
items.subtitle: The park and the Abong-Abong viewpoint

children.text: Arrive at the park entrance and see the tree house and the gardens first.
Go by habal-habal or on foot to the Way of the Cross on Mt. Pulong Bato and enjoy the city view from the cross at the top.
Come back down, have lunch and rest.
Look around the museum (weekdays), the pools and the area around Camp Limbaga.
Go back downtown by jeepney or taxi before dark.

There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Zamboanga International Airport (ZAM). Airlines and schedules change often, so check the latest flights on a booking site.

From the airport, a taxi is the easiest way into the city. A travel guide updated in September 2026 says about ₱100-120 to the City Hall area is reasonable but that drivers often ask ₱150-200, and another blog says some drivers quote a fixed ₱250 to a downtown hotel. Overall, expect roughly
, and agree on the meter or the fare before you ride.
We could not confirm the flight time or fares for this guide.
Jeepneys to Pasonanca leave from a downtown stop (described as being near the Oro Drugstore).
The ride takes about
20–30 minutes
, and fares vary by source at about
, so confirm with the driver.
Look for a jeepney with "Pasonanca" on the windshield. Visitors report getting off in front of the Boy Scout grounds (Camp Limbaga).
You can take a taxi up from downtown, which is convenient if you have luggage or a group. Confirm that the meter is used and the fare before you ride.
Inside the park or toward Mt. Pulong Bato you can use motorcycle taxis (habal-habal). Agree on the price before you board.

Zamboanga is said to show little difference between wet and relatively dry months, but because this is an outdoor park, a day with less rain is better. March–May is generally said to be relatively dry, though we could not confirm firm statistics for this guide.

During the day, early morning and the late afternoon before sunset are best for walking. Midday heat is strong, so bring a hat and water. On weekends local families fill the area around the pools and the tree house.

You can stay in the tree house inside the park, but we could not confirm the booking procedure or rate, so inquire first once your dates are set. Most ordinary travelers stay in a downtown hotel and come up by jeepney or taxi.

There are small eateries, sari-sari stores and charcoal-grilled barbecue stalls in the park and on the way up. Downtown Zamboanga has plenty of seafood restaurants. It is easiest to eat lunch before you go up or to bring snacks.

If you want to sit and rest for a long time, park shelters (kiosks) are reportedly rentable by the day. For a family or group picnic you could use a shelter beside the pools, but confirm the fee locally. Bring your own drinking water and trash bags, and take your trash back with you.
Park entry is free and only individual facilities such as the gardens and the museum charge small fees, so carry plenty of small change.
The museum is said to open on weekdays only, so go Monday to Friday if you want to see it.
Some visitors report that the tree house is not always open. If you want to see the inside, ask in advance.
Visitors report that the condition of the pools varies from day to day. If you plan to swim, look at the water yourself before you decide.
Bring sneakers, a hat, water and insect repellent. With so many trees, mosquitoes are possible.
Confirm jeepney and habal-habal fares before you ride.
When climbing Mt. Pulong Bato, avoid midday and bring plenty of water.
The park is large and signage may be sparse, so ask staff or locals at the entrance where the facilities are.
Combine it with a city tour: the park in the morning and Fort Pilar in the afternoon makes for efficient travel.
The security situation in the Zamboanga area can change. Before you leave, check your government's travel advisory and the latest local news.
Leave the park before dark and avoid quiet, isolated corners after nightfall.
Keep valuables deep inside your bag and do not enter forest paths alone.
The pool water may be cloudy or the pools may be empty, so do not get in if the condition is poor.
Hours and prices vary with local conditions, so check the latest notice.
Some facilities in the park may be aging, so watch the railings and steps.
A 17th-century stone fort on the city's waterfront. After coming down from Pasonanca, it is a good stop to combine into the same day.
The park lies north of downtown, where you will find a market, seafood restaurants and a waterfront promenade.
An island known for its pink-tinged sand beach, reached by boat from a downtown pier. A same-day trip with Pasonanca is tight, so plan them on separate days.

blocks.title: Mt. Pulong Bato and Abong-Abong viewpoint

children.text: A small mountain above the park where you follow the Way of the Cross for a view over the city. Visitors report going there by habal-habal from the park.
